name: Min Cost Permutation (Hard Version)
description: The only difference between this problem and the easy version is the constraints on $$$t$$$ and $$$n$$$. You are given an array of $$$n$$$ positive integers $$$a_1,\dots,a_n$$$, and a (possibly negative) integer $$$c$$$. Across all permutations $$$b_1,\dots,b_n$$$ of the array $$$a_1,\dots,a_n$$$, consider the minimum possible value of $$$$$$\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} |b_{i+1}-b_i-c|.$$$$$$ Find the lexicographically smallest permutation $$$b$$$ of the array $$$a$$$ that achieves this minimum. A sequence $$$x$$$ is lexicographically smaller than a sequence $$$y$$$ if and only if one of the following holds: $$$x$$$ is a prefix of $$$y$$$, but $$$x \ne y$$$; in the first position where $$$x$$$ and $$$y$$$ differ, the sequence $$$x$$$ has a smaller element than the corresponding element in $$$y$$$.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$c$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$, $$$-10^9 \le c \le 10^9$$$). The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1,\dots,a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 10^9$$$). It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output $$$n$$$ integers $$$b_1,\dots,b_n$$$, the lexicographically smallest permutation of $$$a$$$ that achieves the minimum $$$\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n-1} |b_{i+1}-b_i-c|$$$.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1844F2 — Min Cost Permutation (Hard Version) [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
